query: For initially solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles exposed to the premelting and melting regime, the limited understanding of their thermal response prevents clear definition of their usable temperature range and behavior during high-temperature synthesis. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the onset and progression of their phase transition and why? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to the starting baseline, relevant boundary conditions, supporting evidence from prior nanoparticle studies, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu HEA nanoparticles, the onset and progression of phase transition are governed by the formation and growth of a metastable, liquid‐like surface layer that forms due to differential atomic mobilities among the constituent elements. This liquid layer nucleates at temperatures below the bulk melting point, serving as the precursor for full melting.
generation.material_initial_state: Crystalline, solid FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles with uniform elemental mixing.
generation.intervention: Expose the nanoparticles to a controlled heating protocol (e.g., in a thermal plasma jet or a high-resolution in situ TEM heating stage) under an inert atmosphere with a well-defined ramp rate across the premelting regime.
generation.conditions: Apply heating under inert conditions with controlled temperature ramp rates such that the temperature spans from about 70% to 100% of the nominal bulk melting point. Use nanoparticles with sizes where surface effects are dominant (e.g., <50 nm) to emphasize the role of surface diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: A transient, liquid-like surface layer mediated by differential surface mobility and early submelting disorder of the constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Due to variable atomic mobilities and differences in individual melting points within the alloy, atoms at the nanoparticle surface become mobile at lower temperatures than the particle core. This leads to the formation of a thin, metastable liquid-like layer that progressively thickens with increasing temperature, eventually leading to homogeneous melting.
generation.predicted_outcome: Prior to bulk melting, observations will reveal the formation of a disordered, liquid-like film on the nanoparticle surface (detectable by shifts in thermal signatures, changes in diffraction patterns, or in situ imaging). The onset of such a layer will occur at a temperature lower than the full melting point, with its extent increasing as temperature rises.
generation.baseline: Initial state with uniformly crystalline nanoparticles showing no evidence of surface disorder or liquid-like behavior at room temperature.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in nanoparticles (especially <50 nm) under rapid heating conditions and may not extrapolate to larger, bulk samples where volume diffusion and homogeneous melting prevail.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the exact temperature threshold for liquid layer formation and whether similar surface-mediated precursors occur uniformly across all compositional variations within FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform in situ high-resolution TEM combined with differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) on a batch of FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles during controlled heating. Implement two heating protocols varying in ramp rate (slow vs fast) to determine if the appearance and growth of the liquid-like surface layer is heat-rate dependent.
measurements: Real-time imaging to detect the emergence and propagation of a disordered, liquid-like surface film.
DSC data to identify a premelting thermal anomaly corresponding to the surface transition.
X-ray diffraction before and after heating to assess changes in crystallinity and short-range order.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show no evidence of a surface liquid layer (i.e., no localized disorder via TEM imaging, absence of a premelting DSC peak, and uniform crystallinity loss only at the melting point), then the hypothesis that differential surface mobility initiates phase transition is falsified.

Although the CTS technique has demonstrated a remarkable potential in synthesizing HEA NPs in a controlled manner, the process is limited to electrically conductive supports and operated in a batch mode, thus not suitable for industrial-scale production of HEA NPs. To overcome this challenge, new methods building on the CTS technique were reported, such as microwave heating, fast moving bed pyrolysis, and aerosol methods. Very recently, a pulsed/scanning laser ablation method was also reported and demonstrated synthesis of high-entropy materials on various substrates. ## Abstract
AbstractRapid synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA NPs) offers new opportunities to develop functional materials in widespread applications. Although some methods have successfully produced HEA NPs, these methods generally require rigorous conditions such as high pressure, high temperature, restricted atmosphere, and limited substrates, which impede practical viability. In this work, we report laser solid-phase synthesis of CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles by laser irradiation of mixed metal precursors on a laser-induced graphene (LIG) support with a 3D porous structure. The CrMnFeCoNi nanoparticles are embraced by several graphene layers, forming graphene shell-encapsulated HEA nanoparticles. The mechanisms of the laser solid-phase synthesis of HEA NPs on LIG supports are investigated through theoretical simulation and experimental observations, in consideration of mixed metal precursor adsorption, thermal decomposition, reduction through electrons from laser-induced thermionic emission, and liquid beads splitting.
